headline: East End on the 5:52 Ebb: Bass Hold the Rip, Blues Crash the Bait Balls
subhead: New moon current is running harder than it has all summer, and the fish know exactly where to sit and wait for it.
body_markdown:
5:52 a.m., east end, and the ebb's already stacking up against the Sandwich side jetty like it's got somewhere to be. New moon Tuesday means we're building toward the biggest tide swings we'll see all month, and the Canal doesn't do subtle when the moon pulls hard. I stood on the rocks this morning watching four-plus knots of green water peel off the rip and I'll tell you straight — that's the kind of current that separates the guys who show up and the guys who show up at the right minute.

Here's the read for anybody who hasn't fished the ditch in a few weeks. We're past the mackerel run — that show wrapped up in June — and we're into the mid-summer pattern now: bass holding deep on the structure, waiting for the current to sweep bait past them, and bluefish willing to chase anything that moves in the top six feet. The east end rip, right off the herring run outflow toward the Sandwich basin, has been the most consistent stretch. Fish the last two hours of the ebb — that's when the rip really organizes itself into a defined seam instead of just churned-up water — and you want a darter or a Guppy swimming plug worked slow across the seam, right where the moving water meets the slower back-eddy. I had two fish over 30 inches Thursday night doing exactly that, both right at the color change where the sandy bottom drops into the deeper cut.

Daylight hours belong to the bluefish right now, and they're not shy about it. Anybody working topwater off the Scusset side in the last hour of daylight ebb has been into choppers busting bait on the surface — poppers, Hab's Hoo's, anything loud, thrown right into the boils. Just bring wire or heavy fluoro leader because these fish are running eight to twelve pounds and they don't care about your $20 plug.

West end's a different story and it's been trickier. The current there doesn't set up the same defined rip — it's more current seam than boil — and that seam has been shifting depending on how hard the flood is running into Buzzards Bay. Mashnee Island and the cut toward Hog Island have both produced, but only on the last two hours of the flood when the water's really stacking against the rocks. White bucktails, 1 to 1.5 ounce, tipped with a strip of squid or a chunk of mackerel, dragged slow along bottom right where the seam pushes against structure — that's been the presentation. Nothing spectacular, but honest fish, mostly 28 to 34 inches, with a few bigger ones mixed in on the darker tides.

Fluke have been a mixed bag, and I'll be straight with you — the strong current on these new moon tides has been dragging grass and weed through the water column on the flood, which makes drifting bucktails a pain. Best window has been the last hour of the ebb into dead slack, when the water clears up and you can actually keep bottom contact without hauling in a salad every other drift. Try the sandy stretches off Phinneys Harbor and along the edge toward Wings Neck — 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce jigheads, worked with short hops right on bottom. Nothing huge, but a few keepers in the mix, and enough action to make it worth the trip if you time the slack right.

What I haven't seen yet — and I get asked about this every single day at the bait shop — is albies or bonito. Too early. That show doesn't usually open up until the back half of August, sometimes not until Labor Day week depending on how the water in the bay warms. I know guys are itchy for it, especially with the ocean side running warm this year, but there's nothing in the Canal or the Bay side approaches yet that tells me that pattern's close. Save your epoxy jigs for now.

Looking ahead: this new moon is going to keep pushing bigger tide swings through the weekend, which means faster current and a tighter bite window on both ends. If I had one shot this week, I'd take the east end on the last two hours of Sunday morning's ebb — should be running around 5:15 to 6:15 based on the tide progression — because that's when the rip's been most organized and the bass have been most willing to commit. West end guys, watch for the flood to really load up against Mashnee in the late afternoon; that's been the better bite than the morning flood, probably because the water's had all day to warm up over the flats before it pushes through. Bring patience either way. This isn't a week where the fish are just sitting there waiting — you've got to be on the right rock at the right minute, same as it's always been out here.
